summary: We developed an interactive 3D web platform that allows users to explore historical equipment left behind by NASA missions on the Moon and Mars. The platform features realistic 3D environments of both celestial bodies, displaying the locations of historical equipment based on geographic coordinates. Users can explore individual equipment through interactive 3D models, learn about its original mission, understand why it was sent, discover its scientific achievements, and access detailed historical and technical information. Our project addresses the challenge by bringing scattered information about space exploration equipment together in one accessible and interactive platform. It aims to preserve humanity's space exploration heritage, make scientific information easier to understand, and help users rediscover the stories behind the equipment left on other worlds.
details:
**The Last Signal** is an interactive 3D web experience that tells the stories of NASA equipment left on the Moon and Mars. We built it for the NASA Space Apps Challenge to help school-age learners discover what these machines did, why they were sent, and what they taught us.

Visitors choose the Moon or Mars, descend to a landing site, and inspect 3D models of mission hardware in the context of the surrounding terrain. They can follow mission timelines, view archival photographs, and learn about the equipment’s role in each mission. On the Moon, they can discover how Surveyor 3 studied lunar soil and how Apollo 12 astronauts later visited the same lander. On Mars, they can explore how the Pathfinder lander delivered Sojourner, the first rover to operate on Mars.

Our creative approach makes the landing site part of the story. The transition from a view of the whole planet to a close-up of a single machine gives visitors a sense of where each mission happened. From there, the timeline connects what they see to the engineering decisions and scientific discoveries behind it. Our goal is to give students a way to explore space history at their own pace and to give educators an interactive resource for teaching planetary science and engineering.

We developed the site with **TypeScript and React** and built the 3D scenes using **Three.js, React Three Fiber, and Drei**. We used **Vite** for development and builds, **GitHub** for version control, and **Cloudflare Pages** for hosting. NASA mission records and imagery informed the timelines, landing locations, and equipment descriptions.

Our team considered scientific accuracy, readability for younger audiences, and the trade-off between 3D detail and browser performance. We focused on making equipment easy to find and inspect, keeping the mission explanations clear, and supporting both English and Arabic so more students could explore the project.
